description:
Slidebean is a presentation tool for building startup pitch decks. You can use its pitch deck builder and templates to organize your idea, explain what you have learned from customers, and show what you plan to do next. This Slidebean Group Buy listing is a separate offer from SEOGBTools. Check the editing, export, and project access included before you choose a plan.

Start with the decision you want the reader to make

A pitch deck works best when it has one clear job. For an investor introduction, that job might be to earn a first call. For a meeting with a potential partner, it might be to get agreement on a pilot. Write the next step in one sentence before opening a template. It helps you decide which facts belong in the deck and which can wait until someone asks.

Write a plain description of your business. Name the customer, the problem they face, and what your product changes. A scheduling startup might say that it helps small clinics fill cancelled appointments by offering them to patients who are already on a waitlist. The reader can understand the customer and the job in one sentence. The slides can then explain how the product works and show what happened in early trials.

Build the first draft around evidence

Start with the problem. Show a moment the customer recognizes, such as a receptionist calling people one by one after a last-minute cancellation. Then show what changes when the product is used. A short workflow with three steps often does a better job than a long list of features. Give each slide a title that says what the reader should learn from it.

Use your own results on the traction slide. If a pilot included five clinics, state how many took part, when it ran, and what you measured. Keep a clear distinction between sign-ups, active users, and paying customers. Add dates and units to charts. If you have early interviews and no sales yet, explain what those interviews helped you decide and what you will test next.

Explain the market and the business model in simple terms

Start with the type of customer you can reach first. Describe what they already pay for, who makes the purchase decision, and how you expect to reach them. A clinic owner and a hospital procurement team may both need scheduling software, but their buying process can be very different. A focused starting market makes the rest of the story easier to follow.

Give readers enough information to understand how the business earns money. If clinics pay monthly, explain what one subscription covers. If the price is still being tested, label it as a test. When you show a market estimate, include the assumptions behind it. A reader should be able to see how the number was built and which parts are still uncertain.

Use a Slidebean template to make the slides easier to read

Pick a template that fits the story and the time you have to present it. Move or remove any slide that does not help the reader make the next decision. Use a consistent heading style, choose a few colors with strong contrast, and use clear charts where a number matters. Check the deck at the size it will be viewed. Small labels that look readable in the editor can be hard to see on a shared screen.

Keep an editable version and an approved version for sharing. Read through the exported or shared version from start to finish. Check that images have loaded, the order makes sense, and any links work. If the deck includes confidential details, check who can open it before sending the link. Use Slidebean’s official website to review the vendor’s current product and plan details.

Finish with the next step

End with a request the reader can answer. If you want a first investor meeting, include a short contact line and a clear way to reach you. If you are asking for a pilot, state who you want to work with, what the pilot covers, and when you can start. Ask someone outside the project to read the deck. If they cannot explain who it serves and what you want them to do, rewrite those slides before changing the design.

What should I check before choosing Slidebean Group Buy?

Check whether you can edit a test deck, use the template you need, and open or export the final version in the format your audience expects. Find out whether projects stay available after access ends and whether a deck can be kept private. Compare those details with a direct subscription if you need to work with confidential investor files or manage access for a team. Browse the SEOGBTools shop for other presentation and design tools.

Plan the investor deck before designing slides

Open a blank document and write the questions an investor is likely to ask. Who experiences the problem? What have they tried already? Who pays for the solution? How do you reach more customers? What would you do with the money you are asking for? The order of those questions gives you a first draft of the deck. An existing business may lead with results. A team still testing the idea may lead with what it learned about a problem and why the next test is worth running.

Collect the source material in one place. Bring together interview notes, approved screenshots, product metrics, and any calculations you plan to use. Add a date and owner to each item. If the team cannot explain where a claim came from, flag it before it becomes part of a slide. A reader can ask for more detail later. Your job at this stage is to make the main case easy to follow and give the team a way to check its work.

Show what customers do today

Describe the steps someone takes before using your product. In the clinic example, a cancellation arrives by phone. A receptionist checks the waitlist, calls patients, and marks the slot as filled if someone answers. Explain which part takes time or leaves gaps. Add a real example from an interview or pilot where you have permission to share it. A concrete description helps a reader understand why the problem matters to the people who experience it.

Give the audience the right level of detail. A slide may only need a diagram of the current process. In a meeting, you can explain what happens when the first patient cannot come in. A deck sent by email needs enough words to explain the diagram without a narrator. Try both versions with someone who has never seen your product. Ask them to tell you where the current process breaks down and who has to deal with it.

Show the product in one useful sequence

Pick a single workflow for the product slide. In the clinic example, you could show an open slot, the message sent to eligible patients, and a confirmed booking. Use three readable frames with a caption under each. Crop screenshots to the area that matters and remove any private data. If you are showing a prototype, label it so the reader understands which parts are working today and which are planned.

Choose screenshots that help answer a question. A large dashboard may look impressive, but it is hard to read if there are twelve small panels on the slide. A close-up of the confirmation screen can explain the result in seconds. Give the slide a headline such as “Patients can confirm an open slot from their phone.” Check that the visual supports that headline and that every label stays legible in the presentation.

Build a traction slide that explains what changed

Choose measures that fit the stage of the company. A pilot team might track how many invited clinics started using the product, how many weeks they stayed active, and how many open slots they filled. A business with paid customers might show revenue, renewal rates, or the number of accounts that expanded. Label the time period and the group included in each number. If a chart excludes trial accounts, state that clearly.

Use one main comparison per chart. If you want to show whether clinics used the product more often after onboarding, compare similar weeks and say how many clinics are represented. If one large clinic accounts for most bookings, make that visible in a note or a second chart. A reader should come away with an accurate picture of what the results show and what you still need to learn.

Explain who buys and how you will reach them

Define your first buyer in enough detail to explain the route to a sale. “Small clinics that already use an online scheduler and have a receptionist managing cancellations” is specific enough to test. Decide who starts the conversation and who signs off. A customer may like your idea and still need approval from a practice owner or an IT provider. That detail affects how you plan a pilot and how long it takes to get a decision.

Describe the channels you intend to test. For a new team, that might be introductions through local practice managers, direct outreach to clinics, or a referral from a scheduling partner. Show what happened when you tried a channel and what you plan to measure next. If you have a small sample, say so. An honest account of an early test is easier to discuss than a projection with no record of how it was made.

Compare the alternatives customers already use

Include the real choices customers have today. A clinic might use a paper list, rely on a tool it already pays for, or leave the slot open. Ask customers why they use those options and what would make them switch. Their answers can help you pick the few points that matter on the comparison slide, such as setup time or how well a tool works with the existing scheduler.

Make your comparisons easy to check. If an alternative offers a feature in some plans, avoid suggesting that it never offers it. You can explain what a customer found difficult in its current workflow and demonstrate how your product addresses that problem. If you do not have evidence for a broad claim, show a focused example from your pilot and describe its limits.

Write a funding ask with milestones

Explain what the next phase of work will accomplish. For an early product, that might mean connecting to one common scheduling system, testing onboarding with a set of clinics, and learning how many pilots become paying accounts. Say what your team would need to do first and how you would know whether each step worked. Tie the work to the customer and product evidence you have already shown.

Keep the main slide readable by grouping the planned work into a few lines. Put detailed budgets, hiring assumptions, and longer projections in supporting material. Check that the slide and the model use the same dates, units, and assumptions. If a milestone depends on a partner or outside approval, explain that dependency so readers can understand the schedule.

Adapt the deck for a live pitch and an email introduction

A live pitch can use short titles and large visuals because you are there to explain the details. An email version needs to make sense when read alone. Add a brief caption to each key chart and state the takeaway in the headline. A reader should understand the deck even if they start by skimming the slides. Keep the two versions in one folder so teammates can find the latest approved copy.

Rehearse with a timer and leave room for questions. If you spend most of the meeting explaining the first two slides, simplify the opening. Ask a teammate to interrupt with likely questions, such as what a pilot costs or who signs the contract. Keep detailed answers in an appendix so you can respond without making the main presentation too long.

Check the finished presentation before sharing

Open the deck on another device and check that the slides fit the screen. Review every chart title, unit, and legend. Try all links and confirm that contact details are current. Read the first and last slide in sequence. The first should tell the reader what the business does. The last should explain what the team wants the reader to do next.

Ask a reviewer to identify the most convincing claim and the claim they trust least. If they cannot say what the product does, revisit the introduction. If they understand the product but question the numbers, add dates, units, or a short note about the sample. Keep a record of revisions so you can track which changes addressed feedback and which were simply design choices.

A slide-by-slide outline you can adapt

Use the following outline to turn your notes into a complete first draft. Give each slide a question to answer. The sequence can change as your evidence improves. If you already have a strong result that explains why the business matters, you may want to show that result earlier. If your product takes a little time to understand, give readers enough context before showing the chart that measures its effect.

  1. Opening. Name the business and describe the customer and outcome in one sentence. Include a clean visual of the product if it makes the offer easier to grasp. Save longer company history for the team or appendix slide.
  2. Problem. Show one situation the buyer recognizes. Explain who handles it today, how often it occurs in the cases you studied, and what it costs them in time or missed work. State the source of any number.
  3. Solution. Show the few steps that create the result. Make clear whether the workflow is live, in a pilot, or still being built. If a screenshot needs a long explanation, crop to the part that illustrates the change.
  4. Market. Describe the first group you can reach and why you chose it. Explain what would need to be true before you expand to another group. A clear first segment helps the reader judge the plan.
  5. Traction. Show what has happened so far. Use dates and definitions. Explain what the result changed about your priorities, such as improving onboarding before testing a new acquisition channel.
  6. Business model. Show who pays, what they get, and how the payment relates to the product. If an assumption is based on interviews or a limited pilot, label it that way and explain how you will test it.
  7. Team. Highlight experience that connects directly to the work ahead. A short line about shipping an integration or working in the customer’s industry is often more useful than a long list of past roles.
  8. Ask. State the decision you want and the next milestone. Share a contact point and an easy way to follow up. Keep sensitive supporting details in a version you share with the right people.

Use feedback to decide what to revise

After a practice presentation, ask the reviewer to describe the customer, the result, and the next step in their own words. Give them a moment before answering their questions. Their summary shows which parts of the story came through. If two reviewers describe the product differently, read the opening and product slides together. Look for terms the team understands internally but an outside reader could interpret in more than one way.

Separate factual corrections from presentation preferences when you collect feedback. Fix an incorrect date, confusing chart label, or unsupported claim before debating layouts. Then look for repeated comments about the flow. If several people ask how you reach clinics, give that answer more space. If they all understand the process but cannot read a diagram on a laptop screen, enlarge the labels and simplify the visual. Keep a short record of the decisions so the next person can review the final deck without reopening every earlier discussion.

Before the next meeting, open the exact version you plan to share and check the first slide, the evidence slide, and the final request. Have someone else confirm that the charts and links match the approved version. A short final check protects the time you spent refining the story and makes it easier to focus on the conversation during the pitch.

Slidebean pitch deck questions

Can I make a first deck before launching a product?

Yes. Focus on the problem, what you learned from potential customers, and what you plan to test. Label early designs as prototypes and describe which parts have been tested. The deck can explain how you will learn whether the idea is worth pursuing even if you have no revenue data yet.

What should I check if a teammate needs to edit the deck?

Test the editing and sharing workflow with a sample that contains no confidential information. Check who can open the project, who can make changes, and whether you can keep an approved copy. Ask your access provider about these details before putting company information into a workspace.

How should I compare Slidebean with other presentation tools?

Try a problem slide, a product walkthrough, and a chart in each option. Check how long it takes to apply a common design, whether the export looks as expected, and how easy it is for someone else to review. See the SEOGBTools shop if you also need design tools for graphics or presentation assets.
